Example ID: 8375607
QUESTION:
Is the breast best for children with a family history of atopy?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Previous studies reported that breast-feeding protects children against a variety of diseases, but these studies were generally conducted on "high-risk" or hospitalized children.
[1] This paper describes the results of our study on the effects of breast-feeding on rate of illness in normal children with a family history of atopy.
[2] A historic cohort approach of 794 children with a family history of atopy was used to assess the effects of breast-feeding on illness rates.
[3] Family history of atopy was based on allergic diseases in family members as registered by the family physician.
[4] Illness data from birth onwards were available from the Continuous Morbidity Registration of the Department of Family Medicine.
[5] Information on breast-feeding was collected by postal questionnaire.
[6] We then compared rates of illness between children with a family history of atopy who were and who were not breast-fed.
[7] Breast-feeding was related to lower levels of childhood illness both in the first and the first three years of life.
[8] In the first year of life they had fewer episodes of gastroenteritis, lower respiratory tract infections, and digestive tract disorders.
[9] Over the next three years of life they had fewer respiratory tract infections and skin infections.

QUESTION:
Can nonproliferative breast disease and proliferative breast disease without atypia be distinguished by fine-needle aspiration cytology?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Cytologic criteria reported to be helpful in the distinction of proliferative breast disease without atypia (PBD) from nonproliferative breast disease (NPBD) have not been rigorously tested.
[1] Fifty-one air-dried, Diff-Quik-stained fine-needle aspirates (FNA) of palpable breast lesions with biopsy-proven diagnoses of NPBD (34 cases) or PBD (17 cases) were reviewed.
[2] The smears were evaluated for the cellularity, size, and architectural arrangement of the epithelial groups;
[3] the presence of single epithelial cells and myoepithelial cells;
[4] The only cytologic feature found to be significantly different between PBD and NPBD was a swirling pattern of epithelial cells.
[5] A swirling pattern was noted in 13 of 17 PBD cases (76%) and 12 of 34 NPBD cases (35%) (P = 0.008).

[8] Market effects also were detected in demand equations;
[9] relative to adults in the nonfluoridated community, adults residing in the fluoridated community with a large dentist supply received a greater number of restorations, suggesting potential supplier-induced demand from less disease and fewer patients.

Example ID: 10966337
QUESTION:
A short stay or 23-hour ward in a general and academic children's hospital: are they effective?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] We evaluated the usefulness of a short stay or 23-hour ward in a pediatric unit of a large teaching hospital, Westmead Hospital, and an academic Children's hospital, The New Children's Hospital, to determine if they are a useful addition to the emergency service.
[1] This is a descriptive comparison of prospectively collected data on all children admitted to the short stay ward at Westmead Hospital (WH) during 1994 and the short stay ward at the New Children's Hospital (NCH) during 1997-98.
[2] These hospitals service an identical demographic area with the latter (NCH) a tertiary referral center.
[3] The following outcome measures were used: length of stay, appropriateness of stay, rate of admission to an in-hospital bed, and rate of unscheduled visits within 72 hours of discharge.
[4] Adverse events were reported and patient follow-up was attempted at 48 hours after discharge in all cases.
[5] The short stay ward accounted for 10.3% (Westmead Hospital) and 14.7% (New Children's Hospital) of admissions, with 56% medical in nature, 30% surgical, and the remainder procedural or psychological.
[6] Admission patterns were similar, with asthma, gastroenteritis, convulsion, pneumonia, and simple surgical conditions accounting for most short stay ward admissions.
[7] The short stay ward increased hospital efficiency with an average length of stay of 17.5 hours (Westmead Hospital) compared to 20.5 hours (New Children's Hospital).
[8] The users of the short stay ward were children of young age less than 2 years, with stay greater than 23 hours reported in only 1% of all admissions to the short stay ward.
[9] The rate of patient admission to an in-hospital bed was low, (4% [Westmead Hospital] compared to 6% [New Children's Hospital]), with the number of unscheduled visits within 72 hours of short stay ward discharge less than 1%.
[10] There were no adverse events reported at either short stay ward, with parental satisfaction high.
[11] The short stay ward was developed through reallocation of resources from within the hospital to the short stay ward.
[12] This resulted in estimated savings of $1/2 million (Westmead Hospital) to $2.3 million (New Children's Hospital) to the hospital, due to more efficient bed usage.

Is gastric electrical stimulation superior to standard pharmacologic therapy in improving GI symptoms, healthcare resources, and long-term health care benefits?

[0] Severe upper gastrointestinal (GI) motor disorders, including gastroparesis (GP), can consume significant health care resources.

[3] A long-term comparison of patients with devices (n = 9) vs intensive medical therapy (n = 9).
[4] A total of 18 eligible patients with the symptoms of GP reported for 1-year baseline and long-term treatment for 3 years.
[5] Patients with the symptoms of GP were treated by a GES or intensive medical therapy (MED).
[6] GP Symptoms, healthcare resource utilization using investigator-derived independent outcome measure score (IDIOMS) and total hospital (inpatient and outpatient) billing costs.
[7] Gastrointestinal symptoms were significantly different from baseline (F = 3.03, P<0.017) with GP patients treated via GES showing more sustained improvement over 36 months than those treated via MED.
[8] Healthcare resource usage, measured via the IDIOMS, significantly improved at 12, 24 and 36 month follow-up for GES patients (F = 10.49, P<0.001), compared with patients receiving medical therapy, who demonstrated further deterioration.
[9] GP patients treated via GES also proved superior to medical therapy at 24 and 36 months with regard to decreased costs (F = 4.85, P<0.001).
[10] Within group comparisons indicated significantly reduced hospital days for both patient groups;
[11] however, no statistical differences were noted between groups in terms of hospital days.
[12] Three of nine patients in the MED group died primarily from i.v.
[13] none of the GES patients died.

[12] The physician underestimated QoL score in 4/9 domains by a mean of 5.5% and overestimated QoL score in 5/9 domains by a mean of 6.9%.
[13] In particular, physicians underestimated the impact of LUTS on social limitations and emotions (P<0.05).

[0] Fluorodeoxyglucose (FDG) has been reported as a surrogate tracer to measure tumor hypoxia with positron emission tomography (PET).
[1] The hypothesis is that there is an increased uptake of FDG under hypoxic conditions secondary to enhanced glycolysis, compensating the hypoxia-induced loss of cellular energy production.
[2] Several studies have already addressed this issue, some with conflicting results.
[3] This study aimed to compare the tracers (14)C-EF3 and (18)F-FDG to detect hypoxia in mouse tumor models.
[4] C3H, tumor-bearing mice (FSAII and SCCVII tumors) were injected iv with (14)C-EF3, and 1h later with (18)F-FDG.
[5] Using a specifically designed immobilization device with fiducial markers, PET (Mosaic®, Philips) images were acquired 1h after the FDG injection.
[6] After imaging, the device containing mouse was frozen, transversally sliced and imaged with autoradiography (AR) (FLA-5100, Fujifilm) to obtain high resolution images of the (18)F-FDG distribution within the tumor area.
[7] After a 48-h delay allowing for (18)F decay a second AR was performed to image (14)C-EF3 distribution.
[8] AR images were aligned to reconstruct the full 3D tumor volume, and were compared with the PET images.
[9] Image segmentation with threshold-based methods was applied on both AR and PET images to derive various tracer activity volumes.
[10] The matching index DSI (dice similarity index) was then computed.

[2] In each case we applied published criteria for subclassification of FTLD-TDP into FTLD-TDP types 1-3.
[3] Voxel-based morphometry was used to compare subjects with each of the different FTLD-TDP types to age- and gender-matched normal controls (n = 30).
[4] We also assessed different pathologic and genetic variants within, and across, the different types.
[5] Twenty-two subjects were classified as FTLD-TDP type 1, 9 as type 2, and 11 as type 3.
[6] We identified different patterns of atrophy across the types with type 1 showing frontotemporal and parietal atrophy, type 2 predominantly anterior temporal lobe atrophy, and type 3 predominantly posterior frontal atrophy.
[7] Within the FTLD-TDP type 1 group, those with a progranulin mutation had significantly more lateral temporal lobe atrophy than those without.
[8] All type 2 subjects were diagnosed with semantic dementia.
[9] Subjects with a pathologic diagnosis of FTLD with motor neuron degeneration had a similar pattern of atrophy, regardless of whether they were type 1 or type 3.

QUESTION:
Is endometrial polyp formation associated with increased expression of vascular endothelial growth factor and transforming growth factor-beta1?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Endometrial polyp is a common cause of abnormal uterine bleeding, but the etiology and pathogenesis remain unclear.
[1] Vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) is angiogenic, related to thick walled vessels and transforming growth factor-beta1 (TGF-β1) is related to fibrotic tissue, which are characteristics of endometrial polyps.
[2] The primary objective of this study was to find out if endometrial polyp formation is associated with increased expression of VEGF or TGF-β1, or both.
[3] A secondary objective is to determine if the changes are related to steroid receptor expression.
[4] This prospective study compared VEGF and TGF-β1 expression of endometrial polyps and adjacent endometrial tissue in 70 premenopausal women.
[5] The comparison of results was separately made for endometrium specimens obtained in the proliferative and secretory phases.
[6] The results were correlated with the steroid receptors (estrogen receptor and progesterone receptor) expression.
[7] The score of VEGF in glandular cells of endometrial polyps was significantly higher than the score in adjacent endometrium, both in the proliferative phase (P<0.001) and the secretory phase (P=0.03);
[8] the score of VEGF in stromal cells of endometrial polyps was significantly higher than the score in adjacent endometrium only in proliferative phase (P=0.006).
[9] The score of TGF-β1 in glandular cells of endometrial polyps was significantly higher than the score in adjacent endometrium in proliferative phase (P=0.02);
[10] whereas the score of TGF-β1 in stromal cells of endometrial polyps was significantly higher than the score in adjacent endometrium, both in the proliferative phase (P=0.006) and the secretory phase (P=0.008).
[11] There was a significant correlation between the expression of steroid receptors and VEGF and TGF-β1 (Spearman's correlation P<0.001 and P<0.05, respectively).

[8] The association between BMI change and knee pain was independent of radiographic knee osteoarthritis (OA).
[9] The strength of association between BMI and knee pain at Y15 was similar during followup measurements.

[0] The differential diagnosis between essential tremor (ET) and Parkinson's disease (PD) may be, in some cases, very difficult on clinical grounds alone.

[2] Ioflupane, N-u-fluoropropyl-2a-carbomethoxy-3a-(4-iodophenyl) nortropane, also called FP-CIT, labelled with (123)I (commercially known as DaTSCAN) has been proven to be useful in the differential diagnosis between PD and ET and to confirm dopaminergic degeneration in patients with parkinsonism.
[3] The aim of this study is to identify dopaminergic degeneration in patients with PD and distinguish them from others with ET using semi-quantitative SPECT (123)I-Ioflupane (DaTSCAN) data in comparison with normal volunteers (NV), in addition with the respective ones of patients referred as suffering from ET, as well as, of patients with a PD diagnosis at an initial stage with a unilateral presentation of motor signs.
[4] Twenty-eight patients suffering from ET (10 males plus 18 females) and 28 NV (12 males and 16 females) were enroled in this study.
[5] In addition, 33 patients (11 males and 22 females) with an established diagnosis of PD with unilateral limb involvement (12 left hemi-body and 21 right hemi-body) were included for comparison with ET.

[7] Qualitative (Visual) interpretation of the SPECT data did not find any difference in the uptake of the radiopharmaceutical at the level of the S, CN and P between NV and ET patients.
[8] Reduced accumulation of the radiopharmaceutical uptake was found in the P of all PD patients.
[9] Semiquantitative analysis revealed significant differences between NV and ET patients in the striatum, reduced in the latter.
[10] There was also a significant reduction in the tracer accumulation in the left putamen of patients with right hemi-parkinsonism compared to ET and NV.
[11] Patients with left hemi-parkinsonism, demonstrated reduced radioligand uptake in the right putamen in comparison with ET and NV.
[12] Clinical follow-up of 20 patients with ET at (so many months afterwards) revealed no significant change in clinical presentation, particularly no signs of PD.

QUESTION:
Would corrected QT dispersion predict left ventricular hypertrophy in hypertensive patients?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] We explored whether QT corrected dispersion (QTcD) can identify left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) in hypertensives.

[3] Electrocardiogram was performed to measure QTcD.
[4] LVH was present in 42 patients (42%) of the study group, none among controls.
[5] Hypertensive patients had significantly greater indices of LVH and QTcD compared with controls (p<0.001 for all).
[6] Similarly, among hypertensive patients, those with LVH had a significantly greater QTcD compared with those without (p<0.001).
[7] Pearson's correlation coefficient test demonstrated strongly positive correlations between QTcD and the indices of LVH (p<0.001 for all).
[8] Analysis of the receiver operating characteristic curves identified 60 ms as the optimal cut-off value of QTcD that best predicts LVH in hypertensives.
[9] Using this value, QTcD was able to predict LVH with a sensitivity of 92.9% and specificity 98.2%.

Example ID: 23810330
QUESTION:
Is intraoperative neuromonitoring associated with better functional outcome in patients undergoing open TME?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Intraoperative neuromonitoring (IONM) aims to control nerve-sparing total mesorectal excision (TME) for rectal cancer in order to improve patients' functional outcome.
[1] This study was designed to compare the urogenital and anorectal functional outcome of TME with and without IONM of innervation to the bladder and the internal anal sphincter.
[2] A consecutive series of 150 patients with primary rectal cancer were analysed.
[3] Fifteen match pairs with open TME and combined urogenital and anorectal functional assessment at follow up were established identical regarding gender, tumour site, tumour stage, neoadjuvant radiotherapy and type of surgery.
[4] Urogenital and anorectal function was evaluated prospectively on the basis of self-administered standardized questionnaires, measurement of residual urine volume and longterm-catheterization rate.
[5] Newly developed urinary dysfunction after surgery was reported by 1 of 15 patients in the IONM group and by 6 of 15 in the control group (p = 0.031).
[6] Postoperative residual urine volume was significantly higher in the control group.
[7] At follow up impaired anorectal function was present in 1 of 15 patients undergoing TME with IONM and in 6 of 15 without IONM (p = 0.031).
[8] The IONM group showed a trend towards a lower rate of sexual dysfunction after surgery.

Example ID: 23992109
QUESTION:
Is the urinary biomarkers assessment a non-invasive approach to tubular lesions of the solitary kidney?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] The solitary kidney (SK) is currently debated in the literature, as living kidney donation is extensively used and the diagnosis of congenital SK is frequent.
[1] Tubulointerstitial lesions associated with adaptive phenomena may occur early within the SK.
[2] Analysis of the significance of urinary biomarkers in the assessment of tubulointerstitial lesions of the SK.
[3] A cross-sectional study of 37 patients with SK included 18 patients-acquired SK (mean age 56.44 ± 12.20 years, interval from nephrectomy 10.94 ± 9.37 years), 19 patients-congenital SK (mean age 41.52 ± 10.54 years).
[4] Urinary NAG, urinary alpha-1-microglobulin, albuminuria, eGFR (CKD-EPI equation) were measured.
[5] In acquired SK, NAG increased in 60.66%, urinary alpha 1-microglobulin in 16.66%, albuminuria in 55.55% of patients.
[6] Inverse correlation with eGFR presented NAG (R(2 )= 0.537, p = 0.022), urinary alpha 1-microglobulin (R(2 )= 0.702, p = 0.001), albuminuria (R(2 )= 0.655, p = 0.003).
[7] In congenital SK, NAG increased in 52.63%, urinary alpha 1-microglobulin in 5.26%, albuminuria in 47.36% of patients.
[8] In this group, urinary biomarkers correlated inversely with eGFR: NAG (R(2 )= 0.743, p < 0.001), urinary alpha 1-microglobulin (R(2 )= 0.701, p = 0.001), albuminuria (R(2 )= 0.821, p < 0.001).
[9] Significant correlations were found between the urinary biomarkers in both groups.

[4] We collected 23 consecutive cases of suspected carotid FFT seen on CTA (13 men, 65 ± 10 years;

[9] Follow-up imaging confirmed sixteen FFT+ and seven FFT- cases.
[10] Five shape descriptors delineated FFT+ from FFT- cases.
[11] The logistic regression model produced from combining all five shape features demonstrated a sensitivity of 87.5% and a specificity of 71.4% with an area under the ROC curve = 0.85 ± 0.09.
[12] Average accuracy for each classifier ranged from 65.2%-76.4%.

[2] Nineteen patients who received image-guided brachytherapy after concurrent radiochemotherapy were included.

[8] The variations between delivered and prescribed doses at PIBS points were not significant.
[9] However, at International commission on radiation units and measurements rectovaginal point, the delivered dose was decreased by 1.43 ± 2.49 Gy from the planned dose (p = 0.019).
[10] The delivered doses at the four points were strongly correlated with the prescribed doses with R(2) ranging from 0.93 to 0.95.
[11] The movements of the applicator in regard of the PIBS point assessed with the Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine coordinates were insignificant.

[6] Black Caribbean patients, however, showed the opposite effect (OR 1.26, CI 1.09-1.46).
[7] The results for antidepressant use were very similar although the corresponding effect for black Caribbeans was no longer statistically significant (p = 0.07).

[14] Work conditions and context influenced conduciveness for innovation and the extent to which graduates were able to have effect.

QUESTION:
Do healthier lifestyles lead to less utilization of healthcare resources?

NUMBERED CONTEXT SENTENCES:
[0] Governments are urged to determine methods to control the use of medical resources and curb the rise of healthcare costs.
[1] The question is, do health behaviors have an impact on the use of medical resources?
[2] This study aims to identify and understand the difference in the number of outpatient visits and health examinations based on various health behaviors and to determine whether patients seek medical care for illness from the same physicians.
[3] This study used the dataset derived from the Department of Budget, Accounting and Statistics of Kaohsiung, Taiwan in 2005.
[4] Persons older than 15 years were surveyed using an on-site questionnaire.
[5] A total of 2911 persons were enrolled in this study.
[6] Independent t-tests, chi-square tests, one-way ANOVA, multiple linear regression and binominal logistic regression were used in the data analysis.
[7] The regression model for the frequency of doctor visits, health examinations, and whether the same physician is sought for medical care has demonstrated significant correlations with gender, age and education-level variables.
[8] Four health behaviors (i.e., exercise habits, dietary habits, regular blood pressure measurement, drinking habits) exhibited a significant correlation with healthcare utilization (P<0.05).
